content: Frozen shoulder, also known as adhesive capsulitis, is a condition characterized by pain and a significant loss of shoulder motion due to inflammation. The primary symptoms of frozen shoulder include a noticeable reduction in shoulder mobility, persistent pain, and stiffness. In cases where the condition arises without a clear cause, it typically begins with pain. This pain discourages arm movement, which subsequently leads to stiffness and further restriction of motion. Over time, individuals may find themselves unable to perform everyday activities, such as reaching overhead or behind their back. The underlying cause of frozen shoulder involves inflammation of the joint capsule, which contains ligaments that stabilize the shoulder bones. When this capsule becomes inflamed, the shoulder bones lose their ability to move freely within the joint. While frozen shoulder often occurs without a specific cause, certain factors increase the risk of developing the condition. These include cervical disc disease in the neck, diabetes, previous shoulder injuries or surgeries, open-heart surgery, and hyperthyroidism. Diagnosis of frozen shoulder is primarily based on a patient’s symptoms and a physical examination of the shoulder. A hallmark finding is a loss of rotational movement in the shoulder. X-rays may be performed to rule out other conditions, such as arthritis. In some cases, an MRI may reveal inflammation, but there are no definitive imaging findings specific to frozen shoulder. If you experience shoulder pain and stiffness and suspect frozen shoulder, it is important to consult a healthcare provider promptly for evaluation and treatment. Treatment for frozen shoulder typically involves managing pain and restoring motion. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and corticosteroid injections are commonly used to alleviate pain. Combining steroid injections with physical therapy can significantly improve shoulder mobility. However, progress may take weeks, and full recovery can take anywhere from 6 to 9 months. Physical therapy is intensive and requires daily commitment. If left untreated, frozen shoulder often resolves on its own within approximately two years, with minimal long-term loss of motion. However, addressing underlying risk factors, such as diabetes or thyroid disorders, is essential to optimize recovery. Surgical intervention may be considered if non-surgical treatments fail. Under anesthesia, the healthcare provider may manipulate the shoulder to release scar tissue and restore motion. Alternatively, arthroscopic surgery can be performed to cut tight ligaments and remove scar tissue. Post-surgical pain blocks may be used to facilitate participation in physical therapy. Recovery from frozen shoulder generally involves a favorable prognosis. With therapy and NSAIDs, most individuals regain shoulder motion and function within a year. Even without treatment, the condition often resolves spontaneously within 24 months. However, physical therapy must continue for weeks or months after surgery to prevent recurrence. Treatment outcomes may be suboptimal if physical therapy is not well-tolerated. Potential complications of frozen shoulder include persistent stiffness and pain despite therapy. Additionally, there is a risk of arm fractures if excessive force is applied during surgical manipulation of the shoulder. Preventing frozen shoulder involves seeking medical attention promptly if shoulder pain limits your range of motion for an extended period. Early intervention can prevent the progression to stiffness. For individuals with diabetes, maintaining good glycemic control can reduce the likelihood of developing frozen shoulder.
